# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–29 (Complete – Updated 2026-10-13)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Spring of eighth year after Waterloo, continuing into summer. Year is 1830 (French Revolution year). John Sedley deceased (died peacefully, buried at Brompton). Mr. Osborne deceased (four days after stroke). Major Dobbin appointed executor. Rawdon governs Coventry Island. Georgy established as heir.
- **Locations**: London (multiple districts); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate (market town); Pumpernickel (German principality); Ostend (seaside resort, now party residence in "exceedingly dear and uncomfortable house"); Hampshire (Dobbin's rented country place "the Evergreens," near Queen's Crawley).

## Rebecca's Seduction and Integration (Chapters 27–28)
**Encounter and Manipulation**: At Pumpernickel Stadthaus gaming, Rebecca (Madame de Raudon, formerly with Rawdon Crawley) encountered Jos Sedley. Led him to Room No. 92, Elephant lodging-house. Through calculated seduction—hiding degradation evidence, offering tender looks, claiming heart first beat at his presence—convinced Jos she was virtuous and wronged. Revealed true nature to Max and Fritz (Schoppenhausen students): bohemian, boastful, planning wine and theatre rather than respectability. Had falsely advertised Leipzig concert; won money at trente-et-quarante using young Georgy.

**Dobbin's Opposition**: Dobbin called her "the little minx," mistrusted her, recalled Rawdon was "confounded blackleg" who cheated George, remembered separation scandal. Jos resented Dobbin's superiority; stormy colloquy followed. Becky arrived with meagre baggage; Amelia embraced her warmly, flung Dobbin "an angry look—the most unjust and scornful glance" of her life. **FACT: Dobbin had spent fifteen years devoted to Amelia; she had grown accustomed to trampling on him but did not wish to marry him—only to keep him.** Dobbin departed with haughty bow.

**False Narrative and Household Integration**: Becky claimed child "torn from her arms shrieking" by Rawdon's cruelty; bore poverty and neglect; driven to demand separation when Rawdon asked her sacrifice fair fame for Marquis of Steyne advancement. Within week, Jos became "sworn slave and frantic admirer." Becky discovered how to soothe Emmy: praised Dobbin constantly, told her she had behaved cruelly toward him, made Georgy write constantly to Major. Changed habits—no more torn collars, rouge-pot suspended, spirit-and-water indulged only privately.

**Jos's Miniature and Amelia's Regret**: Boxes from Leipzig arrived. From papers box, Becky took gentleman's miniature in pencil, face painted pink, riding on elephant—Jos's miniature. Jos delighted; Emmy tired and unwell. Amelia made aware of Dobbin's movements through Georgy's correspondence. William wrote "in a manner so unconstrainedly cold" that Amelia "felt now in her turn that she had lost her power over him." He was free. "He had left her, and she was wretched." She brooded, reproached herself for "having flung away such a treasure."

**Dobbin's Career and Summer Revelations**: Dobbin joined --th regiment at Chatham. Promoted to Lieutenant-Colonel; Colonel Sir Michael O'Dowd advanced to Major-General with indication Dobbin should become Colonel of distinguished regiment. During summer evenings at Coldcombe, Emmy told Georgy that William was "best man in all the world"; reminded Georgy he owed everything to Dobbin's benevolent care; that William had defended young George at school; that George trusted William above all men.

**Dobbin's Final Speech and Rejection**: William told Amelia: "I have loved you and watched you for fifteen years in vain...You are not worthy of the love which I have devoted to you...I will bargain no more: I withdraw...Good-bye, Amelia!" He broke the chain by which she held him, left with "head on his breast"; never looked back as carriage passed under Amelia's window. Georgy burst out crying. Emmy cleared away Dobbin's books (German dictionary with "William Dobbin, --th Reg.," guide-book) and stored them with her work-box, desk, Bible, prayer-book under pictures of two Georges.

## Chapter 29 – Ostend Crisis and Revelation
**Persuasion to Ostend**: Doctor von Glauber convinced Jos that both he and Emmy needed summer at Ostend. Becky came "as a matter of course" in Jos's fine barouche. At Ostend, scores of Becky's acquaintances cut her; Amelia, who "knew nobody, was not aware of the treatment."

**Disreputable Company**: Major Loder (unattached) and Captain Rook (late of the Rifles) obtained introduction to Jos's household. They invaded dinner-table, "laughed and drank for long hours." Emmy inspired with "intolerable terror and aversion"; they paid "tipsy compliments," leered, made "advances that filled her with sickening dismay." **"A couple of ruffians were fighting for this innocent creature, gambling for her at her own table."** Amelia sent secret letter "to a friend whom she had on the other side of the water"—she looked "very much flushed and agitated" afterward.

**Becky's Cruelty and George's Infidelity Revealed**: Becky reasoned: "She must go away, the silly little fool...She shan't marry either of these men." Marched before Amelia, surveying her with "contemptuous kindness": demanded she marry or face ruin. Then revealed George Osborne was "that selfish humbug, that low-bred cockney dandy...who had neither wit, nor manners, nor heart." **"The man was weary of you, and would have jilted you, but that Dobbin forced him to keep his word. He owned it to me...He made love to me the week after he married you."**

**KEY FACT ABOUT GEORGE**: Becky produced letter: "You know his handwriting. He wrote that to me—wanted me to run away with him—gave it me under your nose, the day before he was shot—and served him right!"

**Amelia's Transformation**: Emmy's head sank; "for almost the last time in which she shall be called upon to weep in this history, she commenced that work." Internal analysis: "Was she most grieved because the idol of her life was tumbled down...or glad because the barrier was removed which modesty had placed between her and a new, a real affection? 'There is nothing to forbid me now,' she thought. 'I may love him with all my heart now.'"

## The Reconciliation and Marriage (End of Chapter 29)
**Dobbin's Arrival**: Two mornings later, despite rain and wind, Amelia insisted on walking Dike with Georgy. English steamer appeared; Georgy spotted through telescope: "There's a man lying down, and a—chap in a—cloak—Hooray!—it's Dob, by Jingo!" Amelia's heart fluttered. "Of course he would come; what could he do else but come?"

**Reunion**: As gentleman in old cloak stepped ashore, "A lady in a dripping white bonnet and shawl, with her two little hands out before her, went up to him...she had altogether disappeared under the folds of the old cloak, and was kissing one of his hands with all her might." She murmured "forgive—dear William—dear, dear, dearest friend—kiss, kiss, kiss."

**Marriage and Departure**: Becky, "satisfied with her part in the transaction," claimed "particular business" took her to Bruges; never presented herself before Colonel Dobbin and his bride. Only Georgy and Jos present at marriage ceremony. Emmy told William: "Never speak of that day again," asking his account of Glorvina and Peggy O'Dowd instead. William joked: "If you hadn't sent for me, who knows what Glorvina's name might be now?" Glorvina married Major Posky after his first wife's death. Lady O'Dowd lives in "great splendour at O'Dowdstown" with Colonel Sir Michael (now Major-General). Both declared Dobbin used Glorvina "SHAMEFULLY," but Paris turban appeased Lady O'Dowd's wrath.

**New Life**: Colonel Dobbin quit service immediately after marriage, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire country place, near Queen's Crawley). Lady Jane and Mrs. Dobbin became great friends; perpetual crossing of pony-chaises between Hall and Evergreens. Lady Jane godmother to Mrs. Dobbin's child (christened Jane, by Rev. James Crawley). George and Rawdon (Sir Pitt's son) hunted and shot together, entered same college at Cambridge, quarrelled over Lady Jane's daughter. Match between George and Miss Crawley was "long a favourite scheme of both matrons," though Miss Crawley inclined toward her cousin. Sir Pitt (lost both Parliament seats after Reform Bill) resided at Queen's Crawley, failed in health, prophesied Empire's ruin. Jos preferred continental life, declined housekeeping with sister and husband; Becky returned to comfort him "just for a few days."

## Final Character States
- **Amelia & William**: Married, reconciled; Amelia's idol shattered but barrier to true love removed; William achieved his objective of fifteen years.
- **Rebecca**: Architect of revelation, absent from marriage; remained with Jos on continent; unchanged nature.
- **Jos**: Enslaved to Becky; preferring continental life.
- **Georgy**: Son of Amelia and William; befriended Rawdon; in love with Lady Jane's daughter.
